title: The raven croaks
hookLine: when a raven croaks an omen, remember no sign has power over your will (Enchiridion 18)

cards: A raven calls from a rooftop just as someone sets out on a journey. In Epictetus' world, that harsh croak could be read as a warning, an omen about the trip ahead. The handbook gives that moment a whole section.
Modern life has its own versions. The text that just says, we need to talk. The dream that leaves a bad taste all morning.
The black cat, the broken mirror, the gloomy forecast for the big day. Something small shows up, and it feels like a message about everything.

teach.b: When a raven croaks an unlucky omen, Epictetus says in section eighteen, don't let the impression carry you away. Instead, divide it at once, and say to yourself: none of this is a sign for me.
It may be a sign about my poor body, or my property, or my reputation, or my children or my wife. But not about me, the part that chooses. Notice he doesn't say omens are nonsense.
Elsewhere in the handbook he treats consulting a diviner as something people did, with its own proper limits, and that comes up in a couple of weeks.

teach.h: NO SIGN FOR ME, ONLY MY OUTER THINGS.
teach.b: His point is narrower: whatever a sign might mean for the things outside you, it can't reach your will. Then the surprising turn.

teach.h: EVERY SIGN IS GOOD, IF I WISH.
teach.b: For me, he says, every sign is a good one, if I want it to be. Whatever comes of it, it's up to me to draw some benefit from it.
A bad harvest, a lost case, a scandal: each one is material for patience or courage or honesty. The raven can croak whatever it likes.

The text that says we need to talk often just means a talk. The bad dream was a dream. Even when the sign is right and trouble comes, the sorting still holds: it touches the outer pile, not the inner one.
A look back at the week: ataraxia, Crates, the leash, the banquet, Paul beside the weeping, the actor, and today the raven. Seven ways of keeping the inner pile your own.

how: Some Stoic practitioners meet a bad omen or ominous news by reminding themselves that it concerns outer things, not their own choices, and asking what good they can draw from what comes.

o: a dream that shows the future exactly as it'll be
a curse someone places on you to bring bad luck
a sign read as a warning about what's coming

games.q: the raven croaks — tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus says all omens are nonsense
he says no sign can reach your will; he doesn't mock divination.
he says every sign can be a good one for you, if you wish
whatever comes, it's up to you to draw benefit from it.
Epictetus says a sign may concern your body, property, name or family
but not you, the part that chooses.

games.q: a raven croaks as you set out. what does Epictetus have you say?
o: turn back; the day is cursed.
this is no sign for me, only my outer things.
games.why: divide it at once: it may concern your body, property or name, but not you. and whatever comes, you can benefit from it.

practice: Bring to mind one bad omen from this week, a message, a dream, a feeling about tomorrow, and let it croak once in your mind.
Sort it the way Epictetus does: this might be about my plans, my money, my reputation, not about me, the one who chooses. Then ask what you could make of it, whatever comes, and let the bird fly off.

wordCard.voice: Omen. Epictetus' answer to a bad sign: it may point at your outer things, never at your will, and whatever comes, you can draw good from it. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: just a bird. A week of keeping the inner pile, done. That's day three hundred fifty.
